content.thinking:
I'm dialing in the gem glow with a moderate emissive intensity so facet shading stays visible, using flat normals and emissive blending to approximate per-facet contrast rather than hand-painting each face. I'm also tallying the gem types, starting with the brilliant-lathe cut.

Now I'm planning the treasure heap's extra props: a cluster of tall glowing crystals rising from one side, a scepter with a gold rod and large gem, a burlap coin sack spilling out, three stacks of tilted coin cylinders, and a glowing rune ring laid flat on the dais beneath the heap using a circular textured decal.

I'm also detailing the dais's mottled stone paint with gold inlay rings at the edges, and working out the chest's dimensions and lid geometry — a half-cylinder vault lid hinged along the back top edge, sized to match the chest body's width, height, and depth.

The single-sided surface would make the inside of the open lid invisible, so I'm considering alternatives: a doubled inner liner with flipped normals, or better, extruding the arch cross-section as a hollow shelled shape along the x-axis, which would need solid end caps to close off the open sides.

Still working out the extrusion geometry...

I need plank seam paint for the arch that runs along the correct axis, deriving angle from position relative to the axis center, and I want paint to be baked in the pose the part has after it's built so the seams follow the closed shape correctly. The chest body planks would work similarly, painted based on position on the box faces.

For the wood paint itself, I'm blending a brown base with noise and grain stripes, darkening narrow seams where the position falls near board boundaries, composing nested paint functions that resolve cleanly. Metalwork comes next: dark steel bands with gold studs, a gold lock plate with a glowing gem keyhole, gold L-shaped corner brackets, and stubby gold ball feet.

For resolution, I'm estimating the painted surface area is roughly 15 square meters, so a 1024 texture gives about 4.6mm per texel which is fine, but I'll bump up to 2048 for crisper detail on the ornate parts. Now I'm setting up the builder with that paint size and defining the root joint, followed by a hinge joint for the lid that aims along the hinge axis.

I'm also considering whether to add a floating relic gem above the treasure pile as a magical accent since joints should really only exist for moving parts, but a hovering glowing gem fits the LoL aesthetic and improves top-down readability, so I'll include a small rotating diamond with orbiting rings as a decorative floating element.

Now I'm working out the heap geometry -- defining the dais, chest footprint, and base height, then laying out the individual treasure mounds by position, radius, and height to build up the pile.

I also want a separate gold heap bulging inside the chest itself, like a flattened dome near the chest top, plus the actual heap mesh built from a plane grid rotated flat and displaced upward by the height function, careful to avoid z-fighting right at the dais edge.

For the paint, I'm going with flat shading so the low-poly facets catch light like real cut gold, using a cellular noise pattern to give the illusion of individual coin shapes with darkened borders and slight hue variation between coins for that hand-painted look.

Now I'm scattering coins across the pile: randomizing x/z within the mound area, computing y from the height field plus a small embed offset, tilting each up to 25° with surface normals, and sizing them chunky (~5.5-11cm) for visual exaggeration. I'm budgeting around 330 scattered coins at low octagon resolution (~10.5k triangles total), plus a few standing/leaning coins tilted more steeply for variety.

I'm picking a tint palette dominated by golds with some silver mixed in, planning to multiply a grayscale coin texture by these tints across merged material groups. I'm designing the coin face texture as an SVG with concentric rings, a star emblem, and small dot details, then mapping that onto the cylinder cap using polar UV coordinates.

I'm sizing the texture so stroke widths stay crisp, then working out how the cylinder's side UVs sample the texture column for shading. Beyond the main heap, I'm placing three small coin stacks plus a toppled stack near the front, and scattering around 28 gems of varying cut types across the pile at different heights.

For gem geometry, I'm using lathe profiles with varying segment counts to produce different cut styles — 8 segments for round brilliants, 6 for hexagonal, 4 for square/emerald cuts, combined with non-uniform scaling to get rectangular facets.

Writing lathe profile points...

Then for placement, I'm positioning gems so they sit partially embedded in the heap surface with random tilt rotations to look naturally scattered.

For merging I'm applying each object's transform matrix to its geometry, then converting to non-indexed and recomputing normals for faceted shading, keeping coins and gems in separate merge groups since they share compatible UV attributes within each type.

Each merged group becomes a single part with a shared material per colour, then gets a glow pass applied. I'm budgeting around 40 flat colours to stay under texture limits, and planning goblets as lathe geometries with gold shading profiles, built as separate small parts.

Plotting the goblet outline...

I'm also thinking through decorative details: a ring of gem spheres placed around the bowl using trig math mapped to the lathe frame, plus a rim band in a contrasting jewel color, with all the gem transforms merged into a single list.

Then for a tilted goblet, I need to figure out positioning since the lathe's local origin sits at a chosen point with y running along a near-horizontal axis vector—I'll estimate the placement so the rim touches naturally and verify with the preview tool before adding engraved paint patterns like diamond stripes based on height and angle.

Beyond that, I'm planning a coin trail spilling from a tipped goblet's mouth, a silver palette variant with bluish cel-shaded metal, and a standing goblet filled with gems positioned near the bowl's rim. I'm also sketching crown dimensions with a banded base and spikes, sizing a heroic exaggerated version larger than the standard one.

Now I'm sizing the crown relative to the chest (about 0.4 diameter against a 0.9 wide chest) and positioning it tilted on the heap near the front-left, embedding its lowest point into the slope. I'm also deciding on the spike pattern, alternating tall and small points for a fantasy look.

For each spike, I'm shaping a curved outline that flares outward with a sharp tip, applying a slight outward tilt so the spike leans naturally, then giving it thickness and a beveled edge before adding a gem near the tip.

Still writing crown geometry...

Now I'm planning the scepter lying across the pile: a gold rod with spiral paint and banded sections, following a path computed from the heap's height function so its ends embed naturally into the pile, topped with a gemmed finial.

For the orb finial, I'm adding a gold sphere, a glowing lathed diamond gem, and four spike prongs oriented along the rod's direction using a quaternion-based aim helper to build consistent transform matrices for merging gem geometry into the scene. Next I'm positioning a sack of coins on the left-front of the dais, keeping it within the dais radius.

Now I'm designing the coin sack itself: a lathe profile that bulges outward then necks in with a flared open top, revealing a flat ring of merged coins sitting inside the mouth. I'm adding a rope tie around the neck as a closed sweep curve and a woven burlap texture painted procedurally with a sine-based grain pattern at high resolution, then starting on a pearl necklace.

I'm draping around 28 merged pearl spheres along a path that follows the heap's surface height, with a teardrop pendant gem hanging at the lowest point. For the chest itself I'm adding an iron plinth base, vertical front straps with studs, a gold lock hasp with a glowing cyan keyhole, and planning decorative gold filigree decals for the front panels.

I should add nail dots using merged spheres on the iron bands, and work out the chest straps as boxes across the front with the lid arch bands built from extruded ring arcs sitting at offsets near the chest center, checking they stay hidden inside properly.

Now I'm figuring out the arch outline for the lid plates using a D-shaped curve traced in angle from 0 to 180 degrees, picking a radius and height ratio sized against the chest depth to get the lid's curved profile right.

I'm working out hinge placement and rotation math: the lid sits flush when closed, then when opened swings back around a hinge at the rear by roughly 105-110 degrees, so I'm computing the rotated y and z coordinates relative to the hinge point to figure out how high and far back the lid arch ends up.

Checking whether the rotated geometry stays within the dais radius - at 110° the lid's arch top extends to about z=-1.2, which slightly exceeds the 1.12 boundary, so I'm trying a shallower opening angle of 95° to pull it back inside the allowed space.

That gives overall height near 1.0 plus crystals, which seems reasonable. Now I'm positioning the spill heap to overlap the chest front and base, and placing the chest off-center with a tall crystal cluster at the right-back corner for visual balance.

Beyond that I'm figuring out the floating orb's position roughly above the heap, then laying out the crown, goblets, and sack around the heap in plan coordinates, keeping in mind the viewer's left-right orientation relative to the model's axes.

I'm positioning toppled coin stacks and a necklace near the crown, then working out the heap mounds for each treasure cluster—chest spill, crown, goblet, crystals, and a shallow front mound—before setting up the overall grid resolution for the heap.

Now I'm shaping the dais as a lathed stone platform with chunky stepped edges, adding mottled stone paint with a gold inlay ring, and placing a rune decal plane just above the surface to avoid z-fighting with the top step.

Then I'm sketching the crystal cluster as hexagonal lathed shapes with a pointed cone tip, defining each crystal's profile with small radial segments.

Five crystals of varying heights and tilts cluster from a base point, colored cyan and violet with partial glow and flat facet shading. I'm also adding smaller octahedral shards scattered around the base, and starting on a floating gem orb built from an octagonal lathe shape.

Now I'm planning the orbiting rings around the floating orb, made from thin tilted closed sweeps with small beads attached, plus sparkle elements using four-point star cards with strong glow, oriented to face outward from the root.

For the sparkles themselves, I'm deciding to use crossing double-sided card planes standing upright so each star reads correctly from any viewing angle, rather than single flat planes that would vanish when viewed from behind -- roughly twenty-two of these glowing white-gold stars scattered around.

I'm sketching the part budget too: the chest itself runs about 60 parts once I merge the studs, keeping the total well under a thousand. Now I'm starting to write the actual helper code, defining a height function for the gold heap mounds based on distance from each mound center.

Still writing geometry helpers...

I'm setting up a mergeGeometries import and a placement helper that builds transform matrices from position, direction, spin, and scale using quaternions. For coins scattered on a heap, I'm perturbing the surface normal randomly per axis before normalizing to get natural-looking tilts.

Coins now get positioned slightly above the ground along their normal, with some propped upright by raising them based on sine of tilt angle. I'm figuring out distribution via rejection sampling weighted toward the center of the heap, aiming for around 380 coins, with color variation handled through a small palette of gold/silver tint buckets at different probability weights.

Now I'm laying out the chest geometry: defining its center, width, depth, and height, then building it as a hollow box with walls, a floor plinth, and iron trim, working out the exact positions for front and back wall panels.

Shaping the gold surface inside with a bump function so it mounds up toward the center and hides behind the rim, then painting it with the same gold coin-mosaic style and scattering coins and gems across it. I'm also adding a thin gold trim band around the top rim and planning corner L-brackets for the chest's edges.

Switching those corner brackets to solid iron corner posts with gold studs, then placing two front metal straps flanking center, and designing a gold shield-shaped lock plate with a beveled extruded outline on the front face.

Adding a glowing cyan keyhole shape on the plate and a gold hasp tongue extending from the lid joint down over the plate. For the lid itself I'm planning the full bone-chest structure: outer arch shell, crimson liner, end plates, several studded ring bands, a gem on top, and a hasp loop.

Working out the geometry for the end plates and the arched outer shell, generating the arc points for the outer and inner curves to form a closed extrudable polygon...

Then I'm figuring out plank seams for the lid paint texture by computing an angle from the arc center and placing seams at regular angular intervals, like 36° spacing, to simulate wood planks.

Writing wood grain logic...

Now I'm defining a gold paint that blends bronze to bright yellow based on lighting direction, brightens further near the top, and adds subtle noise variation for texture. Next I'll move on to an iron paint variant.

I'm sketching a similar iron paint using dark navy to blue-violet tones for a metallic rim effect, then planning decorative filigree SVG decals—a corner scroll and a center rune motif with gold strokes over darker under-strokes, sized so stroke widths render crisply at raster resolution. Writing SVG path data...

For the chest front panel, I decide to place mirrored scroll ornaments flanking the central lock, generating two separate SVG mirror versions (left and right) rather than using a negative scale transform that would flip the path winding and risk culling, then move on to considering whether the lid needs its own decal plane.

The lid gets a central gem with a rune-extruded gold shield plate sitting flat atop it, built in the lid's local closed-pose frame before final joint posing happens. I also plan where to scatter coins and gems across the chest-gold surface, and position a standing hero goblet on the treasure heap, resting its base against the sloped ground near the chest.

Working out the goblet's exact placement — sinking its foot slightly into the slope and tilting it a few degrees toward the surface normal for a natural resting angle. I'm designing the goblet itself as a chunky lathe profile with a flared rim, then painting on gold with decorative enamel bands like a ruby-red stripe.

I'm adding dark engraving lines near the bowl's midsection and groove rings at specific heights, plus six gemstone studs placed radially outward around the bowl, requiring me to interpolate the bowl's radius at that height to position them correctly.

Next I'm working on a tipped silver goblet lying on its side on the heap, figuring out the axis orientation so the bowl rim rests on the ground while the foot tilts upward, and calculating the base position so the lowest point of the bowl actually touches the ground surface.

For the coins spilling from the goblet's mouth, I'm computing their fall trajectory outward from the rim along the tilt direction with some jitter, landing them on the ground slope plus a few resting inside the bowl. Then I'm positioning the burlap sack leaning against the heap on the left side of the chest, giving it a slight outward tilt.

Now I'm shaping the sack as a lathe-revolved solid with a thick open mouth rim revealing a dark interior where coins pile up, and adding a woven burlap texture using crossed sine patterns for the surface detail.

Since a perfect fine weave would be too small to read at this texture resolution, I'm simplifying the burlap look to a noise-based tan/dark color mix with a visible stitch seam and a patch rectangle for character. I'm checking API details for the lathe geometry and heap mesh, making sure parts default to the root bone before writing the final code.

Since joint proximity could accidentally attach non-lid parts to the lid or orb bones, I'm defining a small helper that explicitly forces the root bone onto every call for extrude and sweep operations, while orb parts get their own bone reference. I'm also working out the orientation and thickness direction for the ring-band extrusion on the lid, centering it along the correct axis.

Now I'm figuring out the chest end plates as D-shaped extruded solids with an outer arc and closing base edge, plus wood coloring and gold band outlines. I'm also sketching out the SVG textures for coin faces and cylinder cap UV mapping, defining the circles, strokes, and star polygon that make up the coin design.

I realize the coin texture needs a fully opaque white background rect rather than transparent corners, since the side strip samples the whole image including corners and would otherwise create alpha holes — the circle inscribed caps are fine as-is. For the gem sparkle texture, I'm using a four-point star polygon with a glowing center to keep its natural coloring.

Now I'm designing the rune ring texture for the dais: concentric cyan circles with gold rune tick accents drawn via a loop, sized to map cleanly onto the circle geometry's UVs within the 1024px texture space in the atlas.

I'm checking texture atlas sizing math -- the 2048² paint sheet plus 1024² ring texture plus smaller coin and misc textures need to pack into a 4096² atlas with gutters, though I'm considering dropping to a 2048² atlas if I shrink the paint sheet to 1024² to fit everything in quadrants.

I settle on 1024 for the paint texture and 512 for the ring SVG, estimating resolution gives roughly 4mm detail across a 12m² painted surface, which is fine since chest decals handle fine detail separately. I'm capping the flat color palette at 64 colors, planning gold filigree as a dark outline stroke under a thinner gold stroke, and starting to write the gem color definitions as a flat lookup table keyed by gem name.

Writing gem geometry builder...

I'm now scattering the gems across the heap, defining keepout zones around the crown, goblets, sack, chest, and crystal so gems don't overlap those objects, then doing the same exclusion logic for coin placement near the chest.

I'm checking whether the heap mound near the chest's front wall actually pokes through the chest geometry, since the mound's radius at that z-position seems to overlap the wall slightly and I need to catch that interpenetration.

Now I'm moving on to the crown transform, setting up a matrix combining position, tilt quaternion, and helper functions for applying points and directions before writing out the full implementation.

Still writing crown geometry...

Six big outward-facing gems around the band, ruby in front. For the crown's overall tilt, I'll set rotation so it tips forward and slightly to the side onto the heap, combining X and Z rotations with the translation.

I'll write a helper function for placing gems with a given geometry type, position, direction, scale, and spin, building base geometries once and reusing them. Then I'll construct the heap mesh as a custom plane geometry before assembling everything into final code to typecheck and preview.

For the heap I'm generating a plane geometry rotated flat, then adjusting vertex positions to center it and set height offsets, followed by computing normals and converting to a flat non-indexed mesh. I'm also designing a procedural coin-mosaic paint shader for the heap using cell-based patterns to create borders and shading that mimic piled coins on the slopes.

Now I'm tuning the gold-coin color variation by cell id, adding occasional silver coins, applying a lighting factor based on surface normals, and layering in an ambient-occlusion-like darkening near the dais edges where height is low.

For the dais itself, I'm painting a mottled stone top with a gold inlay ring near the outer radius, flagstone-style mosaic cells with dark edges on top, darker plain stone on the sides, and considering a rune-decal ring for extra detail.

Placing the decal and adding a glow effect to it so the colored texture illuminates in its own hues. I'm also planning the chest keyhole details and the orb, using a lathed gem geometry in its own bone.

Now I'm working out the orb's double-pyramid shape and positioning, plus the tilted gold rings around it using closed Catmull-Rom sweeps with hexagonal cross-sections.

I also need small glowing spheres as beads orbiting the rings, hinge-role joints for both bones, and sparkle card effects at various frame positions — figuring out the card orientation so it faces along Z with cross-billboarding, varying sizes slightly, and adding glow to the sparkle cards.

Now I'm setting the lid's pose rotation and thinking about dressing up the gold chest interior — maybe adding a glowing light-shaft effect using slender tapered gold cards radiating upward from the chest to suggest treasure glow, since the gold paint itself can't emit light.

Writing SVG triangle gradients...
